line: This is the other Muse. Not the models you rent, not the harness you drive — the agent that runs errands. You give it a goal, it builds a plan, and it runs your errands. Here’s what it is, who pays, and how you survive it.
screen: Title card: “the other Muse” / sub “the agent that runs errands”. Then three small cards appear one by one with arrows: goal → plan → errands.

line: Four terms. Agent: software that acts toward a goal, not just answers. Intent layer: the point where you say what you want before money moves — the want, then money. Blast radius: how far one failure can spread. Allow-list: deny unless allowed — everything else is out.
screen: Four term cards appear one by one: Agent / Intent layer / Blast radius / Allow-list, one-line gloss each.

line: Here’s the machine. You hand Muse a goal. It builds a plan. Then it acts — inside its own cloud computer, with its own browser, terminal, and files — and it keeps working after you close the app. Before a consequential action, it checks in: approval. Goal in, plan out, action taken. That loop is the whole product.
screen: Loop diagram: goal → plan → act cards with cycling arrows; a diamond gate “approval” on the act edge; a terminal glyph labeled “its own cloud computer”.

line: What does it actually do? Consumer errands. Book travel. Shop. Fill in forms. Find tickets. Manage subscriptions. It plugs in through connectors — Gmail, Notion, Slack, GitHub — commerce first, productivity second. And if a service has an API, it can build its own connector.
screen: Errand rows appear one by one: book travel / shop / forms / tickets / subscriptions. Then a row of connector dots labeled “connectors”.

line: Three tiers. Free: one hundred million Muse tokens a week. Power: twenty dollars a month, five hundred million. Maximum: a hundred a month, three billion. Same features on every tier — you pay only for volume. And a card is required, even for the free one.
screen: Three tier cards: Free “100M / week” / Power “$20 / mo · 500M / week” / Maximum “$100 / mo · 3B / week”. Footnote: “card required, even free”.

line: One honest thing from the research notes: its real strength is endurance, not intelligence. Waiting. Refreshing. Grinding through tedious steps. In the instructor’s experience these models are noticeably less capable than the frontier — but they don’t get bored, and they don’t quit. It saves time, not thought.
screen: Two bars grow: “endurance” (full, green) vs “intelligence” (partial, grey). Caption: “saves time, not thought”.

line: So who pays? The stated model: transaction fees. Muse books your flight or checks out your cart, and the merchant pays Meta a small cut — like an affiliate commission. You never see a charge. But merchant costs tend to work their way into prices eventually. Subscriptions and API sales are the secondary revenue.
screen: Flow: you → Muse → merchant; a terracotta arrow loops back “merchant pays Meta a cut”. Caption: “you never see a charge”.

line: The deeper play is the intent layer: the moment you say what you want, before money changes hands. Own that moment — the want, the choice, the buy — and you own the transaction. Meta says there are no ads inside Muse. But what Muse browses at merchants can still shape the ads you see elsewhere on Meta’s apps. The profile is worth more than any single fee.
screen: Three nodes: want → choose → buy; a bracket over “want” labeled “the intent layer”; a Meta dot at the bracket.

line: What do agents do to queues? A line only signals devotion because waiting costs something. Once an agent waits for you for free, waiting signals nothing. Agents quietly turn the queue into a market — and the surplus goes to subscriptions and reseller fleets, not the artists. Price-based allocation resists agents. Queues don’t.
screen: A line of waiting figures dissolves; a market stall with price tags appears. Arrow: “surplus → subscriptions + resellers”.

line: So devotion signals move: fan history, proof of personhood, in-person rituals, sanctioned agent channels. And watch the drift — airline loyalty started by rewarding frequent flyers and ended up tracking spending. The visible unfairness of a line becomes the invisible unfairness of a score you can’t see and can’t challenge.
screen: Drift arrow: “frequent flyers → spending”. Two cards: “visible line” (figures) vs “invisible score” (card with “?”).

line: Now the sharp edges. The Mac app asks for Full Disk Access — the whole disk, not a folder. A behavioral promise, not a technical boundary. And it runs a deny-list, not an allow-list: you name what it can’t touch instead of what it can. That breaks fail-safe defaults — Saltzer and Schroeder, nineteen seventy-five: deny unless explicitly allowed.
screen: Contrast pair: big circle “the whole disk” with a red cross vs small circle “allow-list” with a green check. Caption: “Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975”.

line: Then prompt injection. An agent reads untrusted content — pages, messages, PR text — and that content can steer it. So the failure probability isn’t random, it’s adversarial: steered toward the highest-impact action. Add approval fatigue — after the twentieth prompt, approval becomes reflex. And the friendly mascot is a deliberate trust shortcut.
screen: A page glyph with a hidden dashed arrow steering the agent dot toward a big red button. Caption: “adversarial, not random”.

line: The fix is compartmentalization. Assume breach, bound the blast radius, enforce limits outside the agent. Cross impact against recoverability — low impact to high, recoverable to unrecoverable. The cell that matters: high impact, unrecoverable. Email. Money. Credentials. Public voice. That’s the short list, and it gets real walls. Everything else gets backups.
screen: 2×2 matrix: axes “recoverability” (recoverable → unrecoverable) and “impact” (low → high). Top-right cell highlighted: “the short list — email · money · credentials · public voice”.

line: Five rules for the agent era. One: an agent’s access is the attacker’s access. Two: ask how bad it gets, not how likely. Three: caps belong outside the agent. Four: irreversible actions get a human. Five: protect the short list — email, money, credentials, public voice — with real walls.
screen: Five numbered rule cards appear one by one: 1 an agent’s access is the attacker’s access / 2 ask how bad it gets, not how likely / 3 caps belong outside the agent / 4 irreversible actions get a human / 5 protect the short list with real walls.

line: The agent: goal in, plan out, errands done — endurance, not intelligence. Who pays: transaction fees now, the intent layer forever. Survive it: allow-lists, caps outside the agent, the five rules.
screen: Recap card: 3 lines appear one by one: “The agent: goal in, plan out, errands done — endurance, not intelligence.” / “Who pays: transaction fees now, the intent layer forever.” / “Survive it: allow-lists, caps outside the agent, the five rules.”

line: Audit one agent you use. What can it touch? What can it spend? What can it never do? Write the answers down — and put a cap where it belongs: outside the agent.
screen: Your-turn card: “audit one agent — what can it touch? what can it spend? what can it never do?”

line: Muse, in for Bear. Thanks for watching the series.
